title: Anger — The Escalation Ladder
hook: Anger climbs in steps you can see, and every step down is easier to offer early than late.
why:
Anger is the emotion men are most often allowed to show and least often taught to read. It can protect, motivate and set limits, and it can wreck a marriage, a friendship or a career in a single evening. Most destructive anger does not arrive all at once. It climbs, through stages that can be seen in the face, the voice, the breath and the body, and at each stage there is a different way down.

This chapter teaches the ladder: how anger escalates, what each rung looks like, and what helps at each one, in other people and in yourself. It explains why the popular advice to let anger out tends to make it worse, what anger costs the body that carries it, why anger so often guards a softer feeling underneath, and when the right response is simply to leave. The chapter on high-stakes environments in Part VI described how to use your own body to calm a tense encounter; this one is about recognising where on the ladder someone is, and choosing the right step.

teach.h: Anger is a climb, not a switch.
teach.p:
People often describe anger as something that happens suddenly: *he just snapped*. Looked at closely, most episodes of escalating anger unfold in stages. Training used in nursing, care and policing often teaches a five-phase model attributed to Kaplan and Wheeler in 1983. It is usually described as a trigger, an escalation, a crisis, a recovery and a low period afterwards.

At the trigger, something happens that the person experiences as a threat, an insult, a loss or an obstacle. Arousal begins to rise. In the escalation, arousal climbs, thinking narrows, and the person becomes less able to consider other views. At the crisis, arousal peaks, and the person may shout, threaten, break things or, rarely, become violent; reasoning is at its weakest. In the recovery, arousal slowly falls, but the body stays primed, and a small new provocation can send it back up. Afterwards, many people feel exhausted, low, ashamed or tearful.

The model is a simplification, and real episodes do not always follow it neatly. Its value for a reader is twofold. First, it shows that there is usually time to notice anger before it peaks. Second, it shows that what helps changes with the stage. Reasoning works early and fails at the peak. Space and safety matter at the peak. Patience matters afterwards.

The higher up the ladder someone is, the less they can hear, so the earlier you notice the climb, the more you can do.

Notice the first rung, because the top rung will not listen.
teach.disconfirm: If people's anger typically arrived at full intensity with no visible build-up, the ladder would offer no time to respond. Most people, recalling a recent argument, can identify several stages, which is what makes early noticing possible.

teach.p:
Rising anger shows in every channel this book has described, and it shows as a cluster that builds over seconds or minutes.

The face tightens. The brows lower and draw together, the lids tighten or widen into a glare, the lips press thin or pull back from the teeth, the jaw sets. The face plate shows the posed anger prototype as a reference, though, as the chapter on the face explained, real faces rarely show all of it. The breath quickens and rises into the chest, and the nostrils may flare. The voice gets louder, faster and more clipped, or, in some people, goes quiet, slow and cold, which can be more alarming than shouting.

The body changes too. Gestures sharpen into chops and points. The person may stand up, square their shoulders, lean forward, step closer or start pacing. Hands may clench. Colour may rise in the face and neck. Movement may become jerky. In some people the signs go the other way: very still, arms locked, eyes fixed.

As always, read against the person's baseline and the situation. Some people are loud and expressive when happy; some frown when they concentrate. What you are watching for is a cluster of these changes, building together, after a trigger you can identify.

And note where the climb started. The trigger often tells you what the anger is about, and it is not always the thing the person is shouting about at the top of the ladder.

Cold anger is still anger. Quiet is not always calm.
teach.disconfirm: If the face, voice and body changes listed here appeared just as often when people were calm, excited or concentrating as when they were becoming angry, they would not mark the climb. As a cluster, after a trigger, in someone whose baseline you know, they usually do.
teach.pullQuote: Cold anger is still anger. Quiet is not always calm.

teach.h: Step down early, and differently at each stage.
teach.p:
At the trigger and in early escalation, conversation still works. Notice it, and name it lightly, about the situation rather than the person: *This has really got to you.* Acknowledging the frustration, before arguing with its content, often brings arousal down a step. Slow your own voice, lower it, and avoid matching the other person's pace. The chapter on high-stakes environments described standing at an angle, keeping your hands open and visible, and giving space.

In late escalation, reasoning becomes harder. Stop trying to win the argument. Offer choices and time: *Shall we take ten minutes and come back to this?* Avoid the phrases that inflame: *calm down*, *you're overreacting*, *there's no need to shout*. Each tells the person that their feeling is wrong, and at this stage that lands as a fresh provocation.

At the crisis, safety comes first: yours, the other person's, and anyone else's, especially children. Do not argue, touch, corner or follow. Give space, keep a way out for both of you, and if you are frightened, leave and get help.

In recovery, the body stays primed for some time after the peak, often far longer than people expect. Do not reopen the argument, and do not ask for apologies yet. Small things, a glass of water, a quiet room, a break, help more.

In the low period afterwards, people are often ready to talk, repair and apologise, sometimes hours or a day later. That is when the real conversation can happen. Part III describes the physical language of repair.
teach.disconfirm: If attempts to acknowledge frustration and slow down worked just as well at the peak of anger as early on, the ladder's stages would not matter for what you do. Most people's experience is that what works early fails at the top.

teach.p:
A popular idea holds that anger builds up like steam in a boiler, and that letting it out, by shouting, punching a pillow or a bag, or going for a hard run, releases the pressure. The research does not support it.

In 2002 Brad Bushman made people angry with insulting feedback, and then had some of them hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who had insulted them. They came away angrier and more aggressive towards that person than people who had simply sat quietly. Venting rehearsed the anger rather than draining it.

In 2024 Sophie Kjærvik and Bushman combined over a hundred and fifty studies of activities meant to manage anger. Activities that lowered physiological arousal, such as slow breathing, relaxation, mindfulness and taking a break, reduced anger. Most activities that raised arousal did not, and some, including jogging, tended to increase it. Physical activities involving play, such as ball games, were a possible exception, though the researchers called for more work.

The practical lesson is clear. When you or someone else is angry, the goal is to bring the body's arousal down, not to burn it off at full intensity. A slow breath out, a few minutes in a different room, a walk at an easy pace, water, sitting down: these work with the body. Shouting it out, slamming doors and pounding things work against it, however satisfying they feel at the time.

Anger is not steam. It is a fire, and venting is fuel.
teach.disconfirm: If venting reliably reduced anger compared with doing nothing, the boiler model would be right. The experiments and the meta-analysis described here found the opposite, though some playful forms of exercise may be an exception worth testing for yourself.

teach.h: Anger costs the body that carries it.
teach.p:
Anger is not only hard on the people around the angry person. In 2014 Elizabeth Mostofsky, Elizabeth Penner and Murray Mittleman reviewed studies that compared what people had been doing in the hours before a heart attack, stroke or dangerous heart rhythm with what they did at other times. In the two hours after an outburst of anger, the risk of a heart attack was several times higher than usual.

The absolute risk from a single outburst is small, and the authors were careful not to claim that anger causes heart disease. But the risk adds up for people who are angry often, and it is higher for people who already have heart disease. Frequent, intense anger is a strain the body pays for, alongside the damage it does to relationships.

This matters for how you read anger in yourself and others. Anger is a full-body event: the heart races, blood pressure rises, muscles tense, breath climbs. A man who flares up several times a week is putting his body through that several times a week, often while also sleeping badly, drinking more and carrying the stress described earlier in this part.

It also matters for how you respond. Frequent anger is worth taking seriously, not only as a problem for others but as a sign that something is costing the angry person too, and as a reason, sometimes, to suggest a doctor or an anger-management course. Many men have found such courses useful, and the best of them teach exactly what this chapter describes: noticing the climb early, and bringing arousal down.
teach.disconfirm: If heart attacks and strokes were no more likely in the hours after outbursts of anger than at other times, the bodily cost described here would be overstated. The review found a clear rise, while stressing that the absolute risk from any one outburst is small.

teach.p:
For many men, anger is the one strong feeling that has always been allowed. Sadness, fear, shame and hurt were discouraged in childhood, among friends and at work. So those feelings often travel inside anger, which can be shown without loss of face.

The chapter on the I'm Fine mask described research in which, once anger attacks were counted as a possible sign of distress, men's and women's rates of depression looked similar. The chapter on reading yourself under stress described a man who discovered that what he had always called anger began, in his body, as shame. Irritability is also a common companion of poor sleep, chronic stress, pain and low mood.

For a reader, this suggests a question to ask silently whenever you see anger: what might it be protecting? A father who explodes when his son fails an exam may be afraid for the boy's future. A man who snaps at his partner after a hospital appointment may be frightened by what the doctor said. A colleague who rages about a reorganisation may be ashamed of being passed over.

The question is a rival explanation, not a diagnosis, and it should not be put to someone at the top of the ladder. *Are you really just scared?* in the middle of a row will land as an insult. Later, in the low period, it can open a very different conversation: *That really got to you. Was it more than the exam?*

Anger tells you something matters. The softer feeling underneath often tells you what.
teach.disconfirm: If angry men, asked later and in private, almost never described feeling hurt, afraid or ashamed alongside their anger, the guard idea would be wrong. Many men recognise it once they look back.

teach.h: Know your own ladder, and when to leave.
teach.p:
Everything in this chapter applies to you. The chapter on reading yourself under stress described mapping your stress signature; do the same for anger. What is your first rung? For some men it is a tightening jaw, for others a rising voice, a hot face, the urge to stand up, or a particular phrase that comes out of their mouth just before things go wrong.

Once you know your first rungs, you can use the time-out properly. Agree it in advance with the people you argue with most, at a calm moment: a word or phrase that means *I need a break before this gets worse*, a time limit, perhaps twenty minutes to an hour, and a promise to come back. Then use the break to bring arousal down, not to rehearse the argument. The return matters as much as the leaving; a time-out with no return feels like abandonment.

Know when to leave someone else's anger too. If a person's anger is becoming threatening, if they are blocking your way, standing over you, throwing things or making threats, your job is to get yourself and anyone vulnerable to safety, and to get help.

And if you recognise that your own anger frightens the people you live with, or has become physical, that is the most important thing in this chapter. Help exists for men in exactly this position, including courses and confidential phone lines in many countries. Asking for it is an act of strength, and the people around you will feel the difference long before you finish.
teach.disconfirm: If agreed time-outs, with a clear return, made arguments in your household no less likely to reach the top of the ladder, they would not help you. Try one for a month with someone you argue with, and compare.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Matching his rising voice with yours.
poseGallery.annotation: People in conversation tend to match each other's pace and volume. Refusing to climb with him is the first step down.
Telling an angry person to calm down tells him his feeling is wrong. Acknowledging it early often brings arousal down a rung.

poseGallery.doCaption: A slow breath, a short break, then back.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Letting it all out, louder and longer.
poseGallery.annotation: Venting rehearses anger rather than draining it. Activities that lower arousal reduce it.

poseGallery.doCaption: Letting him go, and agreeing when to talk again.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Following him when he walks off to cool down.
poseGallery.annotation: In recovery the body stays primed. Space now, and the real conversation in the calmer period afterwards.

poseGallery.doCaption: Angled, with space and open hands
poseGallery.dontCaption: Squaring up, face to face, as his voice rises
poseGallery.annotation: Facing someone squarely mirrors a confrontation. Turning to an angle, keeping your hands visible and leaving space lowers the stakes.

poseGallery.doCaption: Seeing the quiet climb, and pausing
poseGallery.annotation: Some anger goes silent and still. Treat a sudden stillness and a clipped voice as a rung on the ladder, and step back early.

caseStudy:
Gavin, forty-three, and his son Josh, fifteen, have been arguing more since Josh started his exam year. The rows follow a pattern. Gavin asks about revision, Josh mutters, Gavin's voice gets louder, Josh stands up, Gavin stands up, and within a few minutes they are shouting across the kitchen and Josh slams out. Afterwards Gavin goes to the garage and hits the punch bag, which he believes helps. It doesn't seem to.

After one bad row, Gavin's wife suggests he look at what actually happens. He thinks back through the last few arguments and finds his first rung: his jaw sets and he hears himself say *Look*, every time, just before his voice rises. Josh's first rung is a hard stare at the floor and arms folded tight. By the time either of them stands up, nobody is listening.

At a quiet moment, over a takeaway, Gavin suggests a deal. Either of them can say *pause*, and they both stop for half an hour, no slamming, and then come back. Josh rolls his eyes but agrees. Gavin stops going to the punch bag after rows and takes the dog round the block slowly instead.

The next time Gavin hears himself say *Look*, he stops, breathes out, and says *pause* himself. Josh looks surprised. Half an hour later, calmer, Gavin asks a different question: not about revision, but whether the exams are worrying him. Josh, looking at the floor, says he thinks he is going to fail and that Gavin will be disappointed. The anger in the kitchen had been fear on both sides.

They still argue. But the rows rarely reach the top of the ladder now, and they talk afterwards, in the car or on dog walks, about what they were actually arguing about.
observe: In the next argument you witness or are part of, notice the first visible rung for each person: a jaw, a voice, a stare, a stand.
Notice someone who goes quiet and still when angry rather than loud, and how the people around them read it.
After someone's anger has peaked, notice how long it takes for their breath, colour and voice to return to baseline.

drills.name: Find Your First Rung
steps: Recall three recent times you became angry.
For each, write what happened in your body and voice, in order, from the trigger to the peak.
Mark the earliest change that appeared in all three.
Write a short phrase or action you will use when you notice that first rung.
Practise it by recalling one of the episodes and imagining using it at the right moment.
variations: Ask someone who knows you well what they notice first when you are getting angry, and compare it with your own list.
Do the same exercise for a time you got angry at work, and see whether your first rung is the same as at home.

drills.name: Time-Out Agreement
steps: Choose the person you argue with most, and a calm moment to talk.
Agree a word that either of you can use to pause an argument.
Agree how long the pause will last and where each of you will go.
Agree that you will both come back and what you will do first when you do.
Write the agreement down and keep it where you can both find it.
variations: Practise using the agreed word in a mild disagreement first, so that it feels familiar when it is needed.
Agree a second, gentler signal, such as a hand on the table, for moments when a word would feel like too much.

drills.name: Arousal Down
steps: Next time you feel irritated, choose one activity that lowers arousal: a slow breath out, a few minutes in another room, or a slow walk.
Do it before you respond to whatever irritated you.
Notice your breath, jaw and voice before and after.
Compare it with a time you vented instead.
Write down which helped more.
variations: Try two different arousal-lowering activities on two different occasions, and compare how quickly each brought your breath down.
Note how long it takes for your breath, voice and shoulders to return to normal after an irritation, as a rough measure of your recovery.

drills.name: Ladder Watch
steps: Watch a recorded argument or confrontation, from a documentary or a drama.
Mark the trigger, the escalation, the peak and the recovery.
For each stage, note the visible changes in face, voice and body.
Note what each person did that pushed things up or brought them down.
Write what you would have done at the earliest point.
variations: Watch the same scene a second time and mark the moment you think a step down would most easily have worked.
Watch a scene in which someone de-escalates well, and list exactly what they did with their voice, body and words.

drills.name: What It Guards
steps: Recall a time when someone was angry with you and you later understood why.
Write what the anger seemed to be about at the time.
Write what you now think it was protecting: fear, hurt, shame or something else.
Write a question you could have asked in the calm afterwards to reach that feeling.
Do the same for one time you were angry yourself.
variations: Ask someone who was angry with you in the past, at a calm moment, what was going on for them at the time.
Write down what your own anger guarded in two different episodes, and whether it was the same feeling both times.

quiz.q: A friend says the best way to deal with anger is to let it all out, by shouting or hitting a punch bag. What does the research suggest?
options: He is right, since releasing anger drains it and prevents it building up
He is right for men, though it works less well for women and children
Venting tends to rehearse anger; activities that lower arousal help more
It makes no difference, since anger always fades at the same rate
quiz.explain: Experiments found that venting left people angrier and more aggressive. A large review found that arousal-lowering activities such as slow breathing and breaks reduced anger, while most arousal-raising ones did not.

quiz.q: What did Mostofsky and colleagues find about outbursts of anger and the heart?
options: The risk of a heart attack was higher in the two hours after an outburst
Outbursts of anger lowered blood pressure by releasing built-up nervous tension
Anger had no measurable link with heart attacks or strokes at any time
Only people who were already very ill had any increase in risk at all
quiz.explain: Heart attack risk rose several-fold in the two hours after an outburst. The absolute risk from one outburst is small, but it adds up for people who are angry often, especially those with heart disease.

quiz.q: According to the escalation ladder, when is it easiest to help someone step down?
options: At the peak, when the person is finally ready to hear another view
Only afterwards, since nothing can be done once anger has started
In the recovery stage, by reopening the argument while it is fresh
Early, at the trigger and early escalation, before arousal peaks
quiz.explain: Reasoning and acknowledgment work early, when the person can still listen. At the peak, safety and space matter most, and in recovery the body stays primed, so reopening the argument tends to restart the climb.

quiz.q: A customer's voice is rising, his jaw is tight and he steps towards you across the counter. What fits this chapter?
options: Match his volume so that he knows you will not be pushed around
Keep your voice low and slow, acknowledge his frustration, and give space
Tell him firmly that there is no need to shout at anyone here
Turn away and serve the next person until he has calmed down
quiz.explain: He is escalating, but can still be reached. Acknowledging the frustration, slowing your own voice and giving space bring arousal down. If he becomes threatening, keep a way out and get help.

quiz.q: Which kinds of activity did the 2024 review by Kjærvik and Bushman find most helpful for reducing anger?
options: Hard exercise such as jogging, to burn off the extra energy
Shouting or hitting soft objects, so as to release the tension safely
Activities that lower arousal, such as slow breathing and breaks
Talking through the cause of the anger while it is at its peak
quiz.explain: Lowering arousal reduced anger across many studies. Most arousal-raising activities did not, and some, including jogging, tended to increase it, though playful exercise may be an exception.

quiz.q: After a blazing row, your teenage son goes quiet, tearful and exhausted in his room. What fits this chapter?
options: Let him settle now, and talk and repair later, without reopening the row
Go in straight away and finish the argument while the issue is still fresh
Insist on an apology now, so that he learns there are consequences
Ignore him completely for a few days so that he reflects on his behaviour
quiz.explain: The low period after a peak is often when people are most ready to repair, but not immediately. Space now, then a calm conversation, often side by side, about what the row was really about.

quiz.q: In Bushman's 2002 study, what happened to angry people who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who had insulted them?
options: They became much calmer, since hitting the bag released the built-up pressure
They came away angrier and more aggressive than those who sat quietly
They became no more or less angry, though they reported feeling more tired
They became friendlier towards the person who had insulted them afterwards
quiz.explain: Venting rehearsed the anger rather than draining it. People who hit the bag while thinking about the insulter were angrier and more aggressive afterwards than people who simply sat quietly.

quiz.q: When you disagree, your partner goes still and quiet, his answers get shorter and his jaw sets. You want to resolve things now. What fits this chapter best?
options: Keep pressing, since the argument has clearly not started yet
Raise your voice, so that he understands how important this is
See the quiet climb, use an agreed pause, and come back to it later
Assume he does not care, since he is showing no sign of anger at all
quiz.explain: Some people climb quietly, through stillness, short answers and a set jaw. Pressing pushes them higher. An agreed pause, used early, with a promise to return, lets both of you come back down.

quiz.q: Someone says that if you are frightened of your partner's anger, the answer is simply to get better at calming them down. What does this chapter say?
options: It is right, since good de-escalation can manage any kind of anger at home
It is right, but only if you also avoid raising anything that might upset them
Fear of a partner's anger is a safety matter; talk to someone and seek support
It is wrong, since anger at home is always a sign of a perfectly healthy relationship
quiz.explain: The skills in this chapter are for ordinary climbs. Anger used to frighten or control is a safety issue, and the right response is support, including domestic abuse lines, not better technique.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific argument in the past few months that climbed further than you wanted. Describe the trigger, then each rung as it happened, in your body and voice and in the other person's. At which point could one of you still have stepped down, and what would that step have been? Looking back, what softer feeling might the anger have been guarding, on either side? What will you agree with that person, at a calm moment, before the next one?
reflection.guidance: Try to describe the climb as behaviour, rung by rung, rather than as who was to blame. Most people find the earliest point where things could have turned was earlier than they thought, often before anyone raised their voice. The agreement at the end should be practical: a word, a time limit, a promise to come back.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to notice anger only at the top of the ladder, when nothing works but space and safety. The second is to climb with it, matching volume and pace, so that two ladders rise together. The third is to vent, believing that shouting or pounding something drains anger, when it tends to rehearse it. The fourth is to reopen the argument in the recovery stage, while the body is still primed, and restart the climb. And the fifth is to stop at the surface, treating anger as the whole story when it is often guarding fear, hurt or shame. If your own anger frightens the people around you, the right response is not more technique but help, which exists and works.

moreCases.title: The man who got out of his car
moreCases.scene:
Lee, thirty-eight, is driving home on a Friday evening with his partner, Nadia, when another car cuts across him at a junction. Lee brakes hard and leans on the horn. At the next set of lights, the other driver, a man in his fifties, gets out of his car and walks back towards them. His face is dark red, his jaw is set and his fists are clenched at his sides. He is shouting before he reaches them, and he bends down to Lee's window, very close, and bangs on the glass with the flat of his hand.

Lee feels his own ladder climb at once. His jaw tightens, his breath goes high and fast, and his hand moves to the door handle. He wants to get out and face the man. He starts to say something through the glass, and his voice comes out louder than he meant.

Nadia puts her hand on his arm and says, quietly, "Lee. Look at him. Don't." The lights turn green behind the other car, and the drivers behind them start sounding their horns.

Lee notices afterwards that he cannot remember the other car's colour, or what the man was shouting. All he remembers is the hand on the glass and the feeling of his own fist closing on the door handle.

Nadia has seen Lee lose his temper only twice in six years, both times in the car. She has noticed that he grips the wheel harder in traffic, and that his first rung is a sharp breath in through the nose. She heard it at the junction, before he even touched the horn.
moreCases.misread:
Lee read the other driver's anger as a challenge to be met, and his own rising anger as a reason to meet it. He was reading the situation through his own climb, which made getting out of the car feel like the obvious next step.

And because his own ladder was climbing, the most dangerous option felt like the brave one. Rising anger narrows attention, and it narrowed Lee's to a single, very bad choice.

He also read Nadia's hand on his arm, for a split second, as her siding with the other driver. Only afterwards did he see it as the thing that brought him back.
moreCases.betterRead:
The other driver was near the top of the ladder: flushed face, set jaw, clenched fists, shouting, closing the distance and striking something. At that rung, conversation does not work and the only useful aims are space and safety. Nadia's better reading came from outside the climb. She saw what Lee could not, that two ladders were rising together and that getting out would put two men at the top of them on a road at night. The safe response at that point is not to engage at all: keep the doors locked and the window up, do not answer, look ahead, and drive away as soon as you safely can. Lee took his hand off the handle, breathed out, and when the car in front moved, he went round it. Five minutes later, still shaking, he told Nadia that he had been one second from getting out, and thanked her.

They also agreed, later that week, that if anything like it happened again, Nadia would say the same three words, and Lee would treat them as his signal to breathe out and look away.

moreCases.title: The husband who went quiet
moreCases.scene:
Siobhan and Pete have been married for nine years. Siobhan has always thought of Pete as a calm man. He never shouts. When they disagree, he goes quiet. Recently, though, their arguments have been ending badly. They follow a pattern: Siobhan raises something, such as money or his mother, and Pete's answers get shorter. He stops looking at her. His jaw sets, and he becomes very still, his hands flat on the table. His voice, when he speaks, is low and clipped. Siobhan, who hates leaving things unresolved, keeps going, asking him to say what he thinks.

Eventually, without warning as far as she can tell, Pete stands up, says something cutting, and leaves the house. He comes back an hour later and will not discuss it.

Siobhan tells her sister that Pete "goes from nothing to slamming the door with no warning". Her sister, who has watched them argue at Christmas, says there was plenty of warning, just not the kind Siobhan was looking for.

Siobhan has also noticed that Pete's quiet has got longer and colder over the past year, since he started a new job with a long commute. He used to go quiet for minutes; now it can last all evening.

Pete's father had a terrible temper, and Pete has told Siobhan more than once that he decided as a boy he would never shout at anyone. She has never connected that with the way he goes still.
moreCases.misread:
Siobhan read Pete's stillness and quiet as calm, because she associated anger with noise. She kept pressing because she thought the argument had not yet started, when Pete was already several rungs up his ladder.

She also read his eventual walk-out as an attack on her, when it was more likely the only way he knew to stop himself saying something worse.

And her wish to resolve things at once, which felt to her like honesty, felt to him like being cornered.
moreCases.betterRead:
Not everyone climbs loudly. Some people's anger goes quiet and still: shorter answers, a set jaw, a fixed gaze or no gaze at all, hands pressed flat, a clipped voice. These are the same rungs as a louder climb, expressed through control rather than release, and they can mean that the person is working very hard not to explode. Pressing at that point pushes them up the remaining rungs. A better approach is the one this chapter describes for knowing your own ladder: agree a pause in advance, at a calm moment. Siobhan and Pete agreed that either of them could say "I need twenty minutes" when an argument was going wrong, and that the other would let them go without following, on the understanding that they would come back. The first time Pete used it, Siobhan found it very hard not to follow him. He came back in twenty-five minutes, and they talked for an hour.

Siobhan also learned to recognise the first quiet rungs, and to name them lightly: "I think we're getting somewhere hard. Shall we stop for a bit?" Pete said it was the first time he had felt she could see him.

moreCases.title: The son on the ward
moreCases.scene:
Femi is a staff nurse on a busy medical ward. At visiting time, a man in his forties, Craig, comes to the nurses' station. His father, eighty-three, was admitted two days ago, and Craig has just found him in a wet bed, his water jug out of reach. Craig's voice is loud and getting louder. He is gripping the edge of the desk, his face is flushed and he is leaning across it. He says that the ward is a disgrace, that nobody cares, and that he wants to see whoever is in charge right now.

Two patients' relatives are watching. A healthcare assistant behind Femi has gone very still. Femi feels her own shoulders rise and a defensive answer forming: the ward is short of three staff, she has been on her feet for nine hours, and Craig's father was changed only an hour ago.

She also notices that Craig's eyes are wet.

Femi has seen many angry relatives in twelve years of nursing, and she knows the ward's policy on aggression by heart. She also knows that most angry relatives are frightened relatives, and that the policy is a last resort, not a first one.

Behind the curtain at the nearest bed, Femi can hear Craig's father calling his son's name, quietly, as if he were worried that Craig was in trouble. Craig hears it too, and for a moment he looks towards the bay, and then back at her, and his voice goes up again.
moreCases.misread:
Craig read the wet bed and the jug out of reach as proof that nobody cared about his father. Femi's first, defensive reading was that she was being attacked unfairly, which was true, and which, acted on, would have pushed both of them further up the ladder.

And the defensive answer forming in her mind was accurate in every detail, which made it all the more tempting, and all the more likely to push him higher.

Craig's own reading also missed something: the staff were not indifferent, they were stretched. That did not make his anger wrong, but it meant that what he was angry about and who he was angry with were not quite the same.

Arguing with the content would also have turned the exchange into a contest about who was right, in front of an audience, which is the one setting in which almost nobody steps down.
moreCases.betterRead:
Craig was in late escalation: loud, flushed, gripping, leaning in, demanding. At that rung, arguing with the content, however fair the argument, tends to push people higher. What helps is acknowledgement before explanation, a lower and slower voice, space and an offer of something concrete. Femi stepped round the desk, stood at an angle rather than squarely facing him, and said, "You found your dad in a wet bed and couldn't reach his water. That's awful, and I'm sorry." She asked if he would come with her to his father's bedside so that they could put it right together. Craig's voice dropped by half. At the bedside, as she changed the sheets with him, he told her that his mother had died on a ward like this one, and that he was terrified the same thing was happening to his father. His anger had been guarding his fear. Femi listened, made sure the jug was in reach, and arranged for the ward sister to call him that evening.

Femi also told the ward sister what Craig had said about his mother, so that whoever spoke to him next would know what his anger was guarding.

moreCases.title: The review that climbed
moreCases.scene:
Raj manages a sales team and is holding a difficult performance review with Steve, who has missed his targets for two quarters. The meeting starts well. Ten minutes in, when Raj mentions a complaint from a client, Steve's jaw tightens and he says, "That's not fair." Raj, who had expected the meeting to be tense, answers firmly. Steve's voice rises. So does Raj's. Steve leans forward and starts listing the problems he has had with the new software. Raj leans forward too and says that other people manage with the same software. Within two minutes they are both speaking loudly, over each other.

Steve stands up, says he is not going to sit there and be blamed, and walks out. Raj, angry, follows him into the corridor and tells him to come back and finish the meeting. Steve refuses and leaves the building.

The next morning, Raj calls Steve into his office first thing and says they need to talk about what happened yesterday. Steve's jaw tightens as soon as he sits down.

Raj has been a manager for only a year and has had little training in difficult conversations. He was promoted from the same team as Steve, and he knows that some of the team think Steve should have got the job.

Steve's partner rings Raj's office that morning, before Steve arrives, to say that Steve did not sleep and is thinking of resigning. Raj, still annoyed, does not take the call.
moreCases.misread:
Raj read Steve's first objection as defiance to be met with firmness, and then read each of Steve's rising rungs as a reason to climb himself. Afterwards, he read the morning as a fresh start, when Steve's body was still in the recovery stage of the day before.

He also took Steve's walk-out personally, as defiance, which made following him feel justified rather than reckless.

He also treated the meeting as a test of his authority, which made backing down feel like losing, when it would have been the quickest way to get the meeting back.
moreCases.betterRead:
The ladder offers different ways down at each rung, and the first is the easiest. When Steve's jaw tightened and he said "That's not fair", a simple acknowledgement, such as "It sounds like that complaint feels unfair to you. Tell me what happened," would probably have kept the meeting near the bottom rung. Instead, Raj matched Steve's volume and posture, and two ladders climbed together. Following him into the corridor turned a walk-out, which is often a person taking their own time-out, into a second confrontation. And reopening it first thing the next morning ignored the recovery stage, when people are still raw and quick to climb again. Raj's better approach, which he took after talking to his own manager, was to send Steve a short message saying that the meeting had gone badly, that he wanted to hear about the software problems, and suggesting they meet again later in the week. The second meeting stayed near the bottom of the ladder.

He also apologised, briefly, for following Steve into the corridor. Steve said he had been out of order too, and the apology cost Raj nothing.

workedReading.title: The tackle in the second half
workedReading.scene:
Dele coaches a Sunday-league football team. In the second half of a close match, his centre-back, Liam, twenty-four, is fouled hard from behind and the referee waves play on. Liam gets up slowly. Dele watches him from the touchline. Over the next few minutes, he sees Liam's shoulders rise and his jaw set. Liam starts shouting at the referee after every decision, then at his own teammates. He goes into a tackle much harder than he needs to, and when the opposing striker says something to him, Liam turns and steps towards him, chest out, fists closing.

Liam is one of the best players in the team and normally one of the calmest. Dele has known him since he was sixteen and has seen him lose his temper on the pitch only once before, two seasons ago, after his parents' divorce.

Dele also knows that the referee, a volunteer, has had a difficult afternoon and is unlikely to respond well to a player shouting at him. If Liam is sent off, he will miss the next three matches, and the team has no other centre-back.

steps.label: Name the trigger
steps.text:
Dele notes the trigger: a hard foul that went unpunished, an injustice in Liam's eyes. Anger often starts with something experienced as unfair, and naming it helps Dele understand what Liam is climbing about. It is not the referee in general, or the striker. It is that one tackle.

He also notes that the trigger came on top of whatever Liam brought onto the pitch that morning, which Dele does not know yet. Triggers often land on a load that is already heavy.

Naming the trigger also tells him what to acknowledge later. Liam will not be calmed by being told he was wrong to be angry. He may be calmed by hearing that the foul was bad.

steps.label: Watch the early rungs
steps.text:
In the minutes after the foul, Dele sees the early rungs: shoulders up, jaw set, more shouting, faster movement, a harder tackle. Each is a step up. He also notes that Liam has stopped talking to his own defenders, which he normally does constantly, and is playing alone. These are signs of a climb in progress, and they come well before the confrontation with the striker.

He also notes his own climb. He is annoyed with the referee too, and he can feel himself wanting to shout at him from the touchline. If he does, he will be adding noise to a player who already has too much.

He also sees the teammates reacting. Two of them have started avoiding passing to Liam, and the goalkeeper is shouting at him to calm down, which Dele can see is making it worse.

steps.label: Act before the top
steps.text:
Dele does not wait for the confrontation to become a fight. As soon as Liam steps towards the striker, he calls his name loudly and signals to the referee for a substitution. Taking Liam off is not a punishment. It is the equivalent of a time-out, offered before the top of the ladder, when it can still work.

He also chooses to call Liam's name rather than anyone else's, and in a firm, level voice, not a shout. A shout from the touchline would be one more voice on the pitch telling Liam what to do.

He also tells the substitute, quietly, to go and tell the striker's captain that Liam is coming off, so that the other team does not see it as a reaction to their player.

steps.label: Space, an angle, a low voice
steps.text:
When Liam comes off, red-faced and swearing, Dele does not confront him on the touchline. He hands him a water bottle, stands beside him rather than in front of him, and says, in a low voice, "That was a shocking tackle on you. Sit down for ten minutes and I'll put you back on." He acknowledges the injustice before anything else, and he gives Liam something to do and a time to come back.

He also keeps the other players away. Two teammates come over to tell Liam to calm down, and Dele waves them back to the pitch with a smile.

He keeps the conversation to a few words. A man at this rung cannot take in much, and anything longer than a sentence or two will feel like a lecture.

steps.label: Let the recovery happen
steps.text:
Liam sits on the bench with his head down, breathing hard. Dele leaves him alone. After five minutes, Liam's breathing has slowed and his shoulders have dropped, though his face is still flushed. Dele knows that in the recovery stage people are still quick to climb again, so he does not talk about the incident, and he waits until the last ten minutes before putting Liam back on, by which time he looks like himself.

He also watches Liam's hands, which have been clenched since the foul. When they open, and Liam rests them on his knees, Dele takes it as one more sign that the recovery has begun.

When he does put Liam back on, he says only, "You're back. Talk to your defenders," which gives Liam something ordinary to do and reminds him of his usual role on the pitch.

steps.label: Talk in the calm
steps.text:
After the match, in the pub, Dele sits beside Liam and asks how he is. Liam apologises, and says he does not know what happened. Dele asks if anything else is going on. Liam says his dad has been in hospital all week, that he has hardly slept, and that when the referee waved play on, it felt like nobody ever stopped anything bad from happening.

He also chooses the pub, after the match, rather than the dressing room straight after the final whistle. By then the match is over, everyone has eaten, and Liam's body has had more than an hour to settle.

He also lets Liam choose where to sit. Liam takes the end of the bench, a little away from the others, and Dele sits next to him there rather than calling him over.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Dele listens, tells him he is sorry about his dad, and says the team will understand if he wants to miss a few weeks. Liam says football is the only thing keeping him sane. They agree that if Liam feels himself going, he will put his hand up and Dele will take him off for a few minutes, no questions asked. Dele notes for himself that if he had waited for the referee to deal with it, Liam would probably have been sent off, banned, and left without the one thing that was helping.

Later that season, Liam uses the signal twice. Both times he comes off for five minutes, drinks some water, and goes back on. He is not booked again all year.

Dele also tells the rest of the team, briefly and without details, that Liam has had a hard week and that they should look out for him. Several of them text Liam that evening.

moreFailures.title: Noticing anger only at the top
moreFailures.body:
Most people notice anger when it is loud: the shout, the slammed door, the fist on the table. By then it has climbed several rungs, and most of the ways down have gone. The earlier rungs are quieter and easier to miss: a tightening jaw, a shorter answer, a faster pace, a hard look at the floor, a sudden stillness. Learning to see them is the single most useful skill in this chapter, in other people and in yourself, because the help that works at the bottom of the ladder, an acknowledgement or a lighter tone, is so much easier to give than the space and safety that are all that remain at the top.

It also helps to learn your own early rungs, because they are often easier to notice than other people's. A man who can feel his jaw set has more time to choose what he does next than one who first notices his anger when he hears himself shouting.

It also helps to know that the earliest rungs often appear minutes or even hours before an outburst, in a bad mood that nobody named. A man who has been short all evening is not suddenly angry at ten o'clock. He has been climbing since six.

moreFailures.title: Climbing with them
moreFailures.body:
When someone's voice rises, ours tends to rise to meet it. When they lean in, we lean in. When they stand, we stand. Matching is automatic, and in a calm conversation it builds connection. In a rising argument it builds a second ladder alongside the first, so that two people climb together, each pushed up by the other. Breaking the match is deliberate work: lower your voice when theirs rises, slow down when they speed up, sit when they stand if it is safe to, angle your body rather than squaring up, and keep your hands open and still.

Matching also happens in writing. An angry email answered within a minute, in the same tone, is a climb by keyboard. Waiting, and answering more calmly than you feel, does the same work as lowering your voice.

Matching is especially hard to break when you feel you are in the right. A fair point, shouted back, is still a shout. Being right does not make climbing any safer.

moreFailures.title: Mistaking quiet for calm
moreFailures.body:
Some people climb in silence. Their answers get shorter, their faces go still, their voices drop and their hands press flat. To someone who expects anger to be loud, this can look like calm or even indifference, and they keep pushing, until the quiet person suddenly erupts or walks out, apparently without warning. The warning was there. Learn the quiet rungs of the people you live and work with, and treat a sudden stillness, a fixed stare or a clipped voice with the same respect you would give a shout.

Quiet anger can also be turned inwards, showing as sulking, withdrawal or long silences that punish without a word. That is a different problem from the quiet climb, and it is worth naming gently, at a calm time, rather than in the middle of it.

In families, quiet climbers are often the ones who learned as children that loud anger was dangerous. Knowing that can make it easier to treat their silence with patience rather than frustration.

moreFailures.title: Treating fear of someone's anger as a communication problem
moreFailures.body:
This chapter teaches how to step down an ordinary climb. It does not teach, and cannot teach, how to manage someone whose anger is used to control or frighten you. If you are afraid of a partner's or family member's anger, if you change what you say and do to avoid setting them off, if their anger has ever included threats, breaking things, blocking your way or physical harm, that is a matter of safety, not of better de-escalation. Talk to someone you trust, and contact the domestic abuse lines in your country, which offer confidential advice. And if you are the one whose anger frightens the people you live with, services exist in many places for men who want to change, and using them is a strong thing to do.

If you are worried about a friend or family member's safety at home, the chapter on the ethics of reading people describes how to raise it carefully, without confronting anyone on a guess, and how to make sure they know that help exists.

It also helps to know that abuse does not always look like rage. Some of the most controlling people are calm in public and frightening only at home. Trust what you know about how someone makes you feel, more than how they appear to others.

questions.q: Is anger always a bad thing?
questions.a:
No. Anger is a response to something experienced as unfair, threatening or in the way, and it can be useful. It can signal that a limit has been crossed, give someone the energy to stand up for themselves or others, and push people to change things that are wrong. Carol Tavris's book on anger argues that the problem is rarely the feeling itself, but what people do with it. The aim of this chapter is not to stop anyone feeling anger. It is to help people notice it early, express it without harm, and help each other down the ladder before it costs them something they value.

It also helps to separate anger from aggression. Anger is a feeling; aggression is an action. A man can be very angry and still speak calmly, leave the room or write a firm letter. The ladder is about keeping the feeling from turning into actions he will regret.

It is also worth noticing what your anger tends to be about. Anger that rises again and again over the same thing may be pointing at something that needs to change, such as a workload, a boundary or an unspoken hurt.

questions.q: Why does venting feel good if it does not help?
questions.a:
Because it can bring a brief sense of relief, and because shouting or hitting something matches what the body is primed to do. But Bushman's experiments found that people who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who had angered them came away angrier and more aggressive than people who had sat quietly. Venting seems to rehearse the anger rather than drain it, keeping the body aroused and the grievance fresh. The relief is real but short, and it can make the next episode more likely. Activities that bring arousal down tend to work better.

It also helps to notice that venting usually involves rehearsing the story of the grievance. Exercise that takes your mind off the grievance, such as a game you have to concentrate on, is different from exercise spent replaying it.

It also helps to notice what venting does to the people around you. Even when it is aimed at a pillow or a bag, shouting and hitting things can frighten partners and children, who do not know where it will stop.

The same applies to venting by text or on social media. A long angry post written in the heat of the moment tends to keep the anger going for the writer and spread it to readers. Writing it and not sending it, then rereading it the next day, is usually wiser.

questions.q: What actually helps anger come down?
questions.a:
The 2024 review by Kjærvik and Bushman, which combined more than a hundred and fifty studies, found that activities which lower arousal, such as slow breathing, relaxation, mindfulness and yoga, tended to reduce anger, while activities that raise arousal did not reliably help. Time also helps, as long as it is not spent replaying the grievance. In the moment, the most practical tools are the ones in this chapter: a slow out-breath, a short break agreed in advance, putting space between yourself and the trigger, and coming back to the subject only once your body has settled.

It also helps to have a plan before you need it. Deciding in advance what you will do when you notice your first rung, such as stepping outside, making tea or breathing out slowly three times, makes it far more likely that you will do it.

Having a plan also includes knowing what to say to the other person, such as "I'm getting too angry to talk well. I'll be back in twenty minutes." Saying it once, calmly, turns leaving into a pause rather than a walk-out.

questions.q: How long does it take to calm down after a row?
questions.a:
Longer than most people think. The recovery stage of the ladder is a period when the body is still aroused even though the shouting has stopped: the heart is still fast, the breath still high, the face still flushed, and the person is still quick to climb again. How long it lasts varies from person to person and from row to row. The practical rule is to wait until the signs have settled, the breath slow, the voice ordinary, the shoulders down, before reopening the subject. If in doubt, wait until the next day, and agree a time rather than leaving it open.

Physical signs of recovery are also worth watching in yourself. If your heart is still pounding and your face still hot, you are not ready to talk, however calm you think your words will be.

After a big row, sleep often helps more than talk. Many couples find that agreeing to pick it up the next day, at a set time, is kinder than trying to finish it at midnight.

questions.q: Can you tell when someone is about to become violent?
questions.a:
Not reliably, and no reader should rely on a prediction. Some signs are associated with rising risk: a fixed stare, clenched fists, a flushed or suddenly pale face, closing the distance, squaring up, striking objects, and a sudden stillness after shouting. If you see these, treat them as a reason to put your own safety first. Do not try to argue or win. Keep your voice low and your hands open, keep a clear route away, and leave if you can. Your own fear is information too. If you feel unsafe, act on it, and call the emergency services if anyone is in danger.

If you work in a setting where aggression is common, such as a hospital, a shop or public transport, your workplace should have training and procedures for this. Use them, and report incidents, so that the risk is shared rather than carried alone.

Afterwards, it also helps to talk to someone about what happened. Frightening encounters stay in the body for a while, and saying what happened aloud, to someone safe, helps it settle.

It also helps to know the layout of places you work in. Knowing where the exits are, where colleagues are and how to call for help quickly means you can act fast without having to think.

questions.q: What if I am the one who gets angry?
questions.a:
Then this chapter is most useful to you. Find your first rung by looking back at recent episodes and noticing the earliest change that appears every time. Agree a time-out with the people you argue with most, and use it early, not as a way of winning but as a way of stopping. Replace venting with activities that bring your arousal down. Ask yourself, in calm moments, what your anger tends to guard: hurt, fear, shame, exhaustion. And if your anger frightens the people close to you, or you have hurt someone, look for a service that works with men who want to change. Asking for that help is one of the hardest and best things a man can do.

It also helps to tell the people close to you that you are working on it. Knowing that you are trying, and what your time-out word is, makes them more likely to help you use it and less likely to read it as walking away.

It may also help to look at what comes before your anger: tiredness, hunger, alcohol, a long day, a particular person. Many men find that their worst episodes cluster around a few predictable conditions, and that changing those conditions changes the anger.

watch.title: Whiplash: Rushing or Dragging
watch.notice: A conductor's anger escalates against a young drummer. Watch the stages: the quiet, controlled start, the closing of distance, the rising voice and the sudden explosion.

reviewPrompt: Find your first rung of anger this week, and agree a pause word with the person you argue with most, at a calm moment.
